response: The function `make_palindrome` takes a string and returns the shortest palindrome that can be formed by appending characters to the end of it. It first calls the helper `is_palindrome`, which checks whether a string equals its reverse (using the slice `string[::-1]`), and if the input already reads the same forwards and backwards it is returned unchanged. Otherwise, it scans suffixes of the string by looping over starting indices `i` and testing whether `string[i:]` is a palindrome, since the first such suffix found (the one starting at the smallest index) is the longest palindromic suffix. Once found, the prefix that lies before that suffix, `string[:i]`, is reversed and appended to the original string, which mirrors the non-palindromic part so the whole result becomes a palindrome. The expression `string[i-1::-1]` reads backward from index `i-1` down to the start, which is the reversed prefix. One detail worth noting is that the loop never returns explicitly if no suffix matches, but in practice the last character alone is always a palindrome, so the loop will always return before it runs out. Also, the reversed-prefix slice relies on `i-1`, so for `i = 0` it would wrap to index `-1`, though that case is unreachable because the function returns earlier when the whole string is already a palindrome.
